title: Haemophilus influenzae — CDC Epidemiology and Prevention of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases (Pink Book), Chapter 8

claims.text: Before vaccines, H. influenzae type b (Hib) was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis and other invasive bacterial disease, primarily in children under age 5.
claims.byte_quote: Before the introduction of effective vaccines, H. influenzae type b (Hib) was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis and other invasive bacterial disease, primarily among children younger than age 5 years; approximately one in 200 children in this age group developed invasive Hib disease.

claims.text: Approximately two-thirds of all Hib cases occurred in children younger than 18 months.
claims.byte_quote: Approximately two-thirds of all cases occurred among children younger than age 18 months.

claims.text: Six capsular polysaccharide serotypes (a through f) of H. influenzae have been described.
claims.byte_quote: Six antigenically and biochemically distinct capsular polysaccharide types have been described; these are designated serotypes a through f.

claims.text: In the pre-Hib-vaccine era, type b organisms accounted for 95% of all H. influenzae strains causing invasive disease.
claims.byte_quote: In the pre-Hib-vaccine era, type b organisms accounted for 95% of all H. influenzae strains that caused invasive disease.

claims.text: In the prevaccine era, up to 60% of invasive disease occurred before age 12 months, with peak occurrence at age 6 to 11 months.
claims.byte_quote: In the prevaccine era, up to 60% of invasive disease occurred before age 12 months, although some infants received passive protection from maternal IgG antibodies passed through the placenta and breastfeeding during the first 6 months of life. Peak occurrence was among children age 6 to 11 months.

claims.text: Meningitis was the most common manifestation of invasive Hib disease, accounting for 50% to 65% of cases in the prevaccine era.
claims.byte_quote: Meningitis, an infection of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, is the most common clinical manifestation of invasive Hib disease, accounting for 50% to 65% of cases in the prevaccine era.

claims.text: Non-type b encapsulated strains can cause invasive disease similar to type b; nontypeable strains are generally less virulent but may cause invasive disease, especially in neonates and adults over 65.
claims.byte_quote: Non-type b encapsulated strains can cause invasive disease similar to type b infections. Nontypeable strains are generally less virulent than encapsulated strains among previously healthy individuals, but may cause invasive disease, particularly among neonates and those older than age 65 years.

claims.text: From 2009-2018, of 36 Hib cases reported in patients under age 5 to ABCs, 33.3% were unvaccinated and 38.9% were undervaccinated.
claims.byte_quote: From 2009–2018, 36 Hib cases in patients younger than age 5 years were reported to ABCs. Two (5.6%) were too young to have received Hib vaccine, 12 (33.3%) were unvaccinated, and 14 (38.9%) were undervaccinated

claims.text: A Gram stain of infected body fluid may show small, gram-negative coccobacilli suggestive of H. influenzae.
claims.byte_quote: A Gram stain of an infected body fluid may demonstrate small, gram-negative coccobacilli suggestive of H. influenzae disease.

claims.text: H. influenzae is a fastidious, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus requiring hemin (X factor) and NAD (V factor) for in vitro growth.
claims.byte_quote: H. influenzae , a fastidious, pleomorphic, gram-negative coccobacillus, requires hemin (X factor) and nicotinamide-adenine-dinucleotide (NAD, also known as V factor) for in vitro growth.
